Week 9: Imposter syndrome

Explain imposter syndrome, see its relevance to your career, identify and reduce its effects, and know the supports.

What it is
  • Introduced by Clance and Imes in 1978. High-achieving women credited their success to luck, not their talents or qualifications.
  • About 70% of men and women feel it at some point.
  • A form of inaccurate self-assessment, linked to perfectionism.
  • Common in medicine because of its high-stakes, evaluative culture.
Triggers and why medicine is at risk
  • Triggers: poor performance or errors, followed by guilt, anxiety and self-doubt.
  • The profession does a poor job of preparing physicians to manage errors or seek support.
Consequences
  • Psychological wellbeing
  • Burnout
  • Clinical performance
  • Career advancement
  • Effectiveness as a teacher
  • Support for learners and peers
How to recognize it

Signs

  • Credits success to luck, not ability.
  • Fears peers will find out they are not good enough.
  • Anxious about every assessment, even low-stakes or formative ones.
  • Withdraws from peers and goes quiet.
  • Deflects compliments and discounts praise.

Risk factors

  • A non-traditional path into medicine or a prior rejection
  • Feeling different from peers (age, school, background)
  • Comparing yourself to peers who seem to answer easily
  • Big transitions, such as starting medical school
The imposter cycle Outside the module
  1. Task
  2. Anxiety
  3. Over-prepare or procrastinate
  4. Success
  5. Credit goes to luck or effort
  6. Praise discounted
  7. Fraud feeling grows, repeat
Reducing its effects Outside the module
  1. Check in on a peer privately and casually.
  2. Listen first. Don't rush to fix it.
  3. Normalize it by sharing your own self-doubt.
  4. Point to concrete evidence of competence.
  5. Point to supports. Escalate for signs of depression or safety concerns.
Students
Schulich Learner Experience Office personal counselling.
Physicians
CMA Physician Wellness Hub.
Likely test angles Outside the module
  • Imposter syndrome is an inaccurate self-assessment. Low confidence that matches real performance is not imposter syndrome.
  • It is not a diagnosis. Burnout is one of its consequences. Depression or safety concerns need escalation, not just reassurance.
  • Errors are the classic trigger, so healthy error disclosure and support-seeking protect against it.
  • It affects how you teach and support others, not only you.

Quick recall

Answer in your head, then check.

An inaccurate one, linked to perfectionism.

Poor performance or errors, with guilt, anxiety and self-doubt.

About 70% of men and women.

Any three of: worse wellbeing, burnout, weaker clinical performance, slower career advancement, less effective teaching, less support for learners and peers.

Week 10: Implicit bias and SDH

Reduce the impact of implicit bias, use the social determinants of health (SDH) and financial supports to plan care, and lower barriers for underrepresented groups.

Why it matters
  • Privilege is largely a function of luck. Many opportunities come from the context we were born into, not hard work.
  • Know your patient's context and meet them where they are, so the plan is one they can follow.
Implicit bias
  • Unconscious, and shaped by all your past experiences. Everyone has it.
  • The space between the biased thought and your reaction is where you have a choice.
  • Mindfulness: focusing awareness on the present moment while calmly acknowledging feelings, thoughts and bodily sensations.
  • Sleep restriction increases implicit bias and influences explicit decisions. You resist bias best when rested, fed and hydrated.
  • The Harvard Implicit Association Test (IAT) helps identify your biases.
  • Under stress, practise self-compassion and remember most patients are doing what they think is reasonable.
When bias acts: System 1 and System 2 Assigned reading
System 1
Fast, automatic. Steers most behaviour. Where bias lives.
System 2
Slow, deliberate. Can override System 1 when you have the resources.

Bias acts most under fatigue, stress, hunger, time pressure and heavy cognitive load.

Reducing bias: 3 strategies Assigned reading
Perspective-taking
Picture the visit from the patient's side, then check it with them.
Partnership-building
Use "we" and "let's", and name shared goals.
Protect cognitive resources
Sleep, eat, manage stress, and fix system pressures.
What bias does to care Assigned reading
  • Women are 3 times less likely to be referred for knee replacement when it is indicated.
  • Black and Hispanic patients get less pain medication despite higher pain scores.
  • COPD is underdiagnosed in women.
  • Patients sense bias, so trust, adherence and follow-up drop.
SDH: why a good plan fails
  • SDH are the social and economic conditions that shape health: income, employment and working conditions, caregiving, access to care, transportation, social support, health behaviours.
  • OHIP covers much of the immediate evaluation, but often not the plan: drugs, physio and other services.
  • A plan fails when the patient can't afford it, has no benefits, can't take time off work, or can't get to appointments. Ask before you prescribe.
Income and coverage supports Outside the module
  • Income sources: employment, Ontario Works (OW), ODSP, CPP Disability, CPP and Employment Insurance (EI). Some come with drug and health coverage.
  • WSIB: work injuries. Covers wages, drugs and physio.
  • Ontario Drug Benefit: 65 and over, under 25 without a private plan (OHIP+), OW or ODSP, long-term care, home care, Trillium.
  • Trillium: high drug costs relative to income, with an income-based deductible.
  • OHIP physio: 19 and under, 65 and over, a hospital stay or day surgery in the last 12 months, or OW or ODSP.
Likely test angles: adapting the plan Outside the module
Newcomer, limited English
Professional interpreter, not family. Plain language and teach-back.
Substance use disorder
Avoid diagnostic overshadowing. Non-opioid care first.
Serious mental illness
Avoid diagnostic overshadowing. NSAIDs raise lithium levels. Ask about ODSP.
Older adult with cognitive impairment
Presume capacity and speak to them directly. Avoid oral NSAIDs. Screen for falls.
No benefits, can't miss work
Lower-cost options, check coverage programs, flexible follow-up.

Quick recall

Answer in your head, then check.

In the space between the biased thought and your reaction.

Increases it and influences explicit decisions.

Perspective-taking, partnership-building, protecting cognitive resources.

WSIB.

Week 12: Environment and health

Describe how environmental and climate concerns contribute to or trigger illness, identify vulnerable patient groups, and prescribe healthy choices that help both patient and local environment.

Core idea
  • Climate change is causing unprecedented impacts on human health.
  • Physicians are at the front line of assessing and managing the direct and indirect effects of planetary health on patients.
Climate and vector-borne disease Outside the module
  • Warmer temperatures expand the range and season of vectors such as ticks and mosquitoes.
  • Lyme disease (tick-borne) is the classic Canadian example. Think of it with fever, myalgias, arthralgias and a large expanding circular rash (erythema migrans) after time outdoors in a tick area.
  • Other climate-linked infections in Canada include West Nile virus.
  • Temperature extremes also cause heat illness and worsen chronic disease.
Environmental and occupational exposures Outside the module
Ultraviolet light
Skin cancer, including melanoma. Sun protection counselling.
Herbicides and pesticides
Linked to some cancers and other illness. Ask about agricultural and occupational exposure.
Solvents
Occupational exposure in labs and industry. Linked to some cancers.

Take an occupational and environmental history: where the patient works, lives and spends time.

Who is most vulnerable Outside the module
  • Older adults and young children
  • People with chronic disease (heart, lung, kidney)
  • Outdoor and agricultural workers
  • People with low income or unstable housing
  • Pregnant people
Diseases of public health significance Outside the module
  • Certain diseases must be reported to public health by law. Lyme disease is one.
  • Reporting drives surveillance and lets public health act.
What you can do Outside the module

With patients: climate resilience

  • Heat warnings, hydration and cooling plans for high-risk patients.
  • Tick checks, repellent and sun protection.
  • Healthy choices that also help the environment: active transport (walking, cycling), a plant-rich diet.

Your clinic or hospital

  • Cut waste and energy use. Choose lower-carbon options, such as inhalers with a lower carbon footprint where suitable.

Advocacy

  • Speak up for policies that protect your patients' current and future health.
Likely test angles Outside the module
  • Fever, lymphadenopathy and a large circular rash after camping: Lyme disease, reportable to public health.
  • Differential for fever with lymphadenopathy in a young adult: mono, cat scratch disease, STIs, lymphoma, local skin infection.
  • Link a disease to its environmental driver: temperature to vectors, UV to skin cancer, pesticides and solvents to cancer.
  • Name a vulnerable group and a prescription that helps both patient and planet.

Quick recall

Answer in your head, then check.

Warmer temperatures expand tick range and season, raising Lyme disease risk.

Erythema migrans: a large, expanding, red circular rash.

UV light, herbicides and pesticides, and solvents.

Active transport (walking, cycling) or a plant-rich diet.
